title: RBAC v2: Incident-time access requirements (SRE notes)
body:
Context
- This doc captures SRE requirements for incident-time operational actions that may require elevated access under RBAC v2.
- Goal: maintain fast incident response while meeting enterprise expectations (least privilege + time-bounded escalation + auditable decisions).
- Scope: Hosted + Dedicated + control plane + Console admin surfaces. Private gets special handling (see “Private constraints”).

Assumptions / definitions
- Normal on-call role: “Developer” (or “Read-only”) plus any team-specific permissions required for routine operations.
- Elevated access: time-bounded “break-glass” session that grants a minimal set of operational permissions (not full Org Admin).
- “Support impersonation” is treated separately from SRE break-glass; may share underlying mechanics but must be gated/approved differently.
- Every elevated action must have audit log coverage: actor, role_ids, policy_version, allow/deny, decision_reason (per audit logging spec).

Why RBAC v2 changes incident response
- RBAC v1 historically allowed broad “admin-ish” access for internal staff, often via feature gates and implicit trust in internal tooling.
- RBAC v2 enforcement will cause on-call tooling / runbooks to fail unless:
  1) permissions are enumerated for incident operations
  2) break-glass workflow is quick enough for SEV response
  3) internal tooling can obtain and present elevated credentials predictably

Principles (SRE perspective)
1) Speed matters: any break-glass path must be <2 minutes from pager to elevated session.
2) Least privilege: elevation should be a named “incident operator” permission set, not equivalent to Org Admin.
3) Safe by default: read-only is the baseline; “mutating” permissions are separate and require explicit step-up.
4) Auditability: must be possible to answer “who did what, why, and under what policy” for every incident.
5) Containment: elevation is time-bounded, scoped (org/project/cluster), and auto-revoked.
6) Reliability: elevation must work when portions of console/control plane are degraded (fallback paths).

Incident-time actions inventory (what on-call actually does)
Below is the current list of actions SREs need during incidents. This is intentionally operational, not product-facing. Proposed mapping to RBAC v2 action names is included as strawman; final taxonomy lives with Authz (Kaitlyn/Jordan).

A. Read-only diagnostics (should be available without break-glass where possible)
- View org/project/service health dashboards (latency, error rates, saturation)
- View request traces / correlation IDs and error payload metadata (but not raw prompts for sensitive customers)
- View model rollout status and recent config changes
- View capacity: GPU pool utilization, queue depths, autoscaler state
- View audit logs for auth failures (RBAC deny spikes during rollout)
- List API keys (metadata only) and key last-used timestamps (no key material)

Notes:
- If any of these require break-glass, on-call will overuse elevation; we should bias toward allowing read-only operational visibility to “Developer” or “Read-only” roles for internal responders, but ensure tenant privacy boundaries.

B. Mutating operational actions (require explicit elevation)
1) Throttle/limit or shed load
- Enable/adjust per-org rate limits / quotas (temporary)
- Apply route-level circuit breakers / denylist patterns (temporary)
- Disable streaming for a specific model route (rare; only as last resort)

2) Rollback / pin / freeze changes
- Rollback model version for a route (Hosted)
- Pause/cancel ongoing rollout (canary)
- Pin to known-good model build or quantization profile

3) Capacity and routing actions
- Move org/project traffic between regions (smart routing override)
- Adjust Dedicated autoscaling policy temporarily
- Add burst capacity / attach additional GPU pool (if available)
- Drain or cordon unhealthy nodes in a dedicated pool (control plane operation; actual infra action may be separate)

4) Credential containment (security-adjacent; requires strict gating)
- Revoke/rotate an API key (org-scoped)
- Disable key creation (org-scoped) during suspected compromise
- Force session invalidation for Console users in an org (rare)

5) Data access & privacy
- Access to raw request/response content should remain heavily restricted; for incident response we generally do NOT need it.
- Exception: with customer approval or explicit “security incident” protocol, security team can authorize limited access. SRE break-glass should not include prompt/response content viewing by default.

C. Administrative / “break-glass plumbing” actions (separate from incident response)
- Grant break-glass session to self (step-up) or to another responder
- Extend break-glass duration (should require secondary approval)
- Create incident record / attach justification in tooling (for audit)

Severity-based expectations
- SEV0/SEV1: allow self-serve break-glass with post-hoc review, but require:
  - ticket/incident ID
  - freeform justification
  - explicit scope (org/project/region)
  - hard TTL (default 60 minutes)
  - auto-notify Security + SRE lead channel
- SEV2+: require approval before elevation OR require secondary approval only for mutating actions (preferred: dual-control for high-risk mutations).

Proposed break-glass workflow changes (requested by SRE)
Current pain points we want to avoid:
- “Ask in Slack, wait for someone with admin access” loops
- One-off manual grants with no consistent audit trail
- Too-broad staff roles that persist beyond incidents

Proposal (mechanics)
1) Time-bounded elevated session (“elevated context”)
- On-call uses internal tool (or Console admin page) to request an elevated session.
- Inputs required:
  - Incident ID (PagerDuty / internal incident doc)
  - Scope: org_id and/or project_id, region (optional), product tier (Hosted/Dedicated/Private)
  - Reason: choose from list + freeform details
  - Requested permission bundle: “incident-ops-read”, “incident-ops-mutate”, “incident-ops-security-containment” (names TBD)
- Output:
  - short-lived token/credential used by internal tooling and Console for permission checks
  - audit events: session_requested, session_granted, session_expired, session_revoked

2) Approval and dual control
- For “incident-ops-read”: no approval (self-serve)
- For “incident-ops-mutate”: self-serve allowed at SEV0/1; otherwise require approval
- For “incident-ops-security-containment” (key revocation/forced logout): always require approval from Security Engineering or designated approver; ideally 2-person rule for some actions (CISO asked for stricter defaults in role definitions discussions)

3) TTL and renewal
- Default TTL 60 minutes. Renewal requires re-asserting incident ID and justification.
- If renewal count > 2, trigger alert to Security to review whether access should be converted into a more formal, approved temporary role.

4) Automatic scoping rules
- Elevation must be scoped; no global/all-org blanket by default.
- Allow emergency “global” scope only behind additional approvals (SEV0 + Security approval) and produce a high-severity audit event.

5) Alerting / monitoring
- Real-time alert when:
  - incident-ops-mutate is granted
  - incident-ops-security-containment is granted
  - any elevated session is used outside business hours (info-level; avoid alert fatigue)
- Daily digest of elevated sessions used (to SRE + Security).

Operational constraints for on-call tooling
We need a design that works with how on-call responds in practice.

Tooling that calls control plane APIs
- Many incident runbooks are CLI-based (internal scripts) and call control plane endpoints directly.
- Requirements:
  - CLI must be able to obtain elevated session creds non-interactively after initial step-up (device auth ok, but don’t require multiple UI hops).
  - Backwards compatibility during migration (dual-eval): script failures must include actionable 403 reason codes.
  - Deterministic error handling: distinguish “not authorized” vs “capacity unavailable” vs “policy cache stale.”

When Console is down / degraded
- If Console is part of the affected surface area, break-glass cannot depend solely on the Console UI.
- Required fallback:
  - internal endpoint or CLI flow that can request elevation (even if Console is down)
  - at minimum, Security team should have a path to grant elevation for SRE via alternate channel with the same audit trail (avoid “manual DB edit” patterns)

Caching/performance
- Authz checks must be low latency on hot paths; for incident tools that batch operations (e.g., list hundreds of projects), permission evaluation must be cacheable.
- SRE request: metrics for authz eval latency and cache hit rates visible in SRE dashboards (tie-in to policy cache PR work).

Human factors
- On-call will copy/paste commands under pressure; permission errors must say exactly what permission is missing and how to request it.
- Don’t make SRE guess whether the right permission is “billing.*” vs “dedicated.autoscaling.*”; provide a “missing_permission” field.

Example incident scenarios (from past quarters) and required access
1) Elevated 5xx on Hosted chat completions in us-east
- Actions needed:
  - view error breakdown and traces
  - shift traffic to us-west (temporary)
  - pause rollout of model version X
- Permissions needed:
  - routing.override (scoped to org/region)
  - rollouts.pause / rollouts.rollback

2) Dedicated customer cannot change autoscaling during deployment regression
- Actions needed:
  - inspect dedicated pool config
  - apply temporary autoscaling policy workaround
- Permissions needed:
  - dedicated.autoscaling.read
  - dedicated.autoscaling.write (elevated)

3) Suspected compromised API key spamming tokens
- Actions needed:
  - identify key_id from logs (metadata)
  - revoke key and block new key creation temporarily
- Permissions needed:
  - api_keys.revoke (elevated + security approval)
  - org_settings.restrict_key_creation (elevated + security approval)

4) RBAC rollout causes deny storm for a subset of orgs
- Actions needed:
  - view authz deny metrics by endpoint
  - identify policy_version and role assignment changes
  - rollback policy bundle or disable enforcement flag (if needed)
- Permissions needed:
  - authz.metrics.read
  - feature_flags.write (high-risk; needs explicit elevation and audit)
  - policy_bundle.rollback (if exposed as operation)

Private deployment constraints (important)
- Private customers may be offline/air-gapped; our incident response is primarily advisory.
- Requirements:
  - no assumption of Redwood staff having direct access to customer private control plane
  - break-glass for Private should exist for customer admins (their own process), not for Redwood SRE by default
  - if a Private customer explicitly configures support access, it must be:
    - opt-in
    - time-bounded
    - customer-auditable
    - revocable by customer
- Action item: ensure policy distribution/version skew in Private doesn’t block customer’s own break-glass (coordinate with Hanae + Private deployment workstream).

Open questions / decisions needed
- What is the minimal “incident-ops-mutate” permission set that still allows SRE to restore service quickly?
- Which actions require secondary approval vs self-serve at SEV0/1?
- Where should “feature_flags.write” live (extremely powerful) and should it be limited to Release Engineering + Security?
- Should SRE have any capability to view customer content (prompts/responses) under any circumstances? (SRE recommendation: default no; exceptions routed through Security incident protocol.)
- How do we handle “global” incidents affecting many orgs without repeated per-org break-glass requests? (Possible: scoped-to-region + product surface, not org.)

Concrete asks to RBAC v2 implementation team
1) Provide a dedicated break-glass session object in audit logs (not just inferred from role changes).
2) Ensure permission errors include:
   - missing_permission (string)
   - decision_reason (enum)
   - policy_version
   - request_id
3) Provide a stable way for CLI tooling to request elevation (API + documented flow).
4) Make read-only operational visibility as broad as possible without exposing tenant content.
5) Support scoped elevation (org/project/region) at evaluation time.

Action items
- Sean: review this list with on-call rotation; mark which items are truly required vs “nice to have.”
- Rafael: propose exact SEV-based approval rules (who approves, where recorded).
- Marcus/Kevin: confirm audit log event schemas for break-glass session lifecycle + alerts.
- Kaitlyn/Jordan: map these operations to RBAC v2 resources/actions and propose default internal roles/policies.
- Connor: ensure migration plan includes runbook updates + training before enforcement.

Notes to self (misc)
- Include at least one game day where we simulate Console outage + need to roll back a model rollout.
- Ensure we have a way to revoke elevated sessions immediately ("kill switch") in case of misuse.
- Ensure policy cache invalidation handles role assignment changes quickly; stale caches during incidents will be brutal.
